extracted.intended_audience: Small law firms and SMMEs (small, medium and micro enterprises) in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and legal standards for obtaining and managing IP rights in South Africa (patents, plant breeders' rights, trade marks/company names, trade secrets, geographical indications and related common-law rights). Aimed at practitioners and small businesses navigating registration, protection, enforcement and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage patent filing (provisional then complete)
rubrics_metrics.description: The South African Patents Act provides for a two-stage filing procedure: (a) an initial provisional patent application can be filed to obtain an official number with a filing date to cover the invention for disclosure/commercialisation by the applicant; and (b) this is followed by a complete patent application which is required to obtain granted rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional gives 12 months to develop, improve or market the invention; complete specification must be filed within 12 months of provisional to avoid lapse. Provisional is not open to public inspection. Individuals may draft and file provisional applications but it is advisable to seek a patent attorney for commercially valuable inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional specification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification must fairly describe the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when invention is conceptual or in development. It secures a filing date and 12 months priority to refine the invention or prepare a complete application. Because a patent can only cover what is disclosed, developments beyond the provisional disclosure may require a subsequent filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete specification must describe the invention in detail and set out a list of claims which define the scope of protection sought under the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete patent application must be drafted and filed by a patent attorney. Claims determine infringement and scope; the applicant should ensure the specification supports the claims. File within 12 months of the provisional filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route options (local, PCT, foreign filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for completion of a provisional patent application include: (1) South African complete patent application (local filing) securing rights in South Africa only; (2) PCT international patent application administered by WIPO covering many contracting states; (3) Direct filing into foreign jurisdictions claiming Paris Convention priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT provides an additional 18 months (after the 12-month priority) before national/regional phase filings are required. Choose route based on desired territorial protection and costs. Use Paris Convention priority when filing directly into foreign jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limited to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application can only cover that which is disclosed in the accompanying specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If developments or modifications go beyond what is covered in an initial document, a second filing will be necessary if those changes are to form part of the subject matter for which protection is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent maintenance (renewal fees and term)
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain a patent, annual renewal fees are payable from the third anniversary of the filing date. The patent will lapse if a renewal fee is not paid within a six-month extension period after the renewal due date. South African patents have a duration of 20 years, which cannot be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track renewal schedule carefully to avoid lapse. There is a six-month extension period after the renewal due date, but failure to pay leads to lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding patent infringement (practical tip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure to take steps to avoid infringing an existing patent: check necessary patent database(s) for the relevant patents; review the claims; and modify your product accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your product cannot use the same combination of features that are covered by the claims of an existing patent. Adding features will not prevent infringement. To avoid infringement, you must leave out one or more features of the patent claim. A patent attorney can assist with searching and advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant breeders' rights (purpose and exclusivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant breeders' rights (plant variety rights) are rights granted to breeders of new plant varieties for protection of their varieties against exploitation and to obtain financial rewards; breeder can be exclusive marketer or license the variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sole right period provides a limited exclusivity (five years for annual crops; eight years for perennial crops) during which licences need not be issued. After expiry of the sole right period, licences must be issued on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: DUS requirement for plant variety grant (Distinct, Uniform, Stable, New)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for granting plant breeders' rights: Plant varieties must have an acceptable variety name and meet the “DUS” (Distinct, Uniform and Stable) requirement and novelty limits (NEW: seed or cutting has not been sold in South Africa for longer than one year; variety has not been commercialised for more than four years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct = clearly distinguishable from any other variety of the same species. Uniform = plants of a variety look similar and are sufficiently uniform. Stable = plants look like the original after repeated cultivation. Follow the statutory timelines for novelty to qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant breeders' rights registration process and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for registration is filed with the Registrar for Plant Breeders’ Rights, which is assessed, and will require samples of the plants for testing; applicants may be individuals or breeding institutions (foreign breeders apply through an agent). Varieties only granted for plants declared in terms of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional protection is available during evaluation if the applicant provides a written undertaking not to sell the varietals until tests are completed. Registration, renewal and duration: PBRs valid for 20 years (annual crops) or 25 years (vines and trees) from date of issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with UPOV and legislative updates
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is a member of UPOV and its plant variety protection system is aligned with the UPOV 1978 convention; the new PBR Act (12 of 2018) coming into force in 2025 is aligned to the 1991 Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alignment to UPOV 1991 would provide for stronger breeder’s rights. Check the operative national regulations and lists of protected species (Regulations Table 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law trade mark rights (first-to-use and passing off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common law rights are established through the actual use of the trade mark in trade, building reputation and goodwill. South Africa recognises unregistered brands used in commerce (first to use). Unregistered trade marks can be enforced under the common law principle of 'passing off' and unlawful competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of a common-law trade mark is more difficult due to evidentiary requirements. Passing off requires proving (1) goodwill and reputation/trade dress, (2) misrepresentation likely to confuse the public, and (3) that the misrepresentation is causing or likely to cause damage to goodwill or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TM and ® symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: TM symbol may be used with an unregistered mark to provide notice that rights in the mark are claimed; the ® symbol can only be used in respect of a registered trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using ® without registration is improper. Use TM for notice when registration has not been obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company name registration constraints and searches
rubrics_metrics.description: The Companies Act prohibits registration of a company with a name the same or confusingly similar to another company name, a registered trade mark, a reserved company name, defensive company name or a well-known trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Registrar of Companies checks the companies register but does not search the Trade Marks register. It is recommended to conduct a trade mark search before registering a company name to avoid objections that can lead to losing the name. An objection is assessed by the Companies Tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive company name registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A defensive company name may be registered for two years (renewable for another two-year period) and requires showing a direct and material interest in protection of the name; transfers require satisfactory evidence of transferee’s direct material interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use defensive names strategically to hold names while preparing business activity, but be prepared to show material interest for registration and for transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and protection criteria for trade secrets (TRIPS/Article 39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets or confidential commercial information (know‑how, formulas, practices, processes, designs, recipes, compilations, customer lists) are protected so long as they are kept secret. TRIPS provides protection for 'undisclosed information' if it: (a) is secret (not generally known or readily accessible to persons who normally deal with this information); (b) has commercial value because it is secret; and (c) reasonable steps have been taken to keep it safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrets have no time limit if secrecy is maintained. Unauthorised disclosure results in unfair competition. Reasonable steps include secure storage, limited access, confidentiality measures and contractual protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical measures to protect trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to identify trade secrets and ensure that confidential information is stored securely with limited access, ensuring confidentiality, and that non-disclosure agreements are in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure employment and service contracts include confidentiality/non-disclosure agreements and that restraint of trade clauses contain a duty not to disclose trade secrets and confidential information. Implement organisational measures (access controls, secure storage, classification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical Indication (GI) definition and collective right
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are names or signs used on products with a specific geographical location or origin, having a quality and reputation linked to the geographical origin. GIs provide a collective right to use the GI, provided the products are produced in that area and produced according to required standards (Code of Practice and specifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Honeybush', 'Rooibos', 'Karoo lamb'. Users within the GI area can prevent non-qualifying producers from using the GI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for GI registration (three elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three elements required for GI registration: (1) the product must be linked to or originate from a specific location; (2) the product must possess a unique quality or characteristic; (3) there must be a link between the quality and the location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI Regulations (Section 17) set out assessment procedure, including priority and objections. Registration gives collective rights and may be enforced against unauthorised use.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI registration, regulation and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: GI registration is provided under various statutes (e.g., Agricultural Products Standards Act, GI Regulations). GIs are valid for an indefinite period until registration is cancelled (unlike trade marks which are renewable ten-year rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI Regulations provide rules for application, assessment, and labelling practice rules for foodstuffs using registered GIs. Non‑compliant use may be an offence and enforceable by the rights holder; enforcement is administered by DALRRD and other agencies as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labelling rules for GIs and regulatory enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A name registered as a South African GI or foreign GI may be used as part of or near the product name (e.g., on labels or in advertisements) subject to strict requirements outlined in the GI regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper use of GIs or prohibited marks may constitute offences (e.g., counterfeiting) and are enforceable. Liquor Products Acts may additionally restrict use of geographical names for liquor sales and export; EU GIs are protected under notices published in the government gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI protection by agreement and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa protects GIs through FTAs/EPAs (e.g., SADC-EU EPA, SACUM-UK EPA) and bilateral agreements; GI rights are territorial and limited to the country/region where protection is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs can be protected nationally, regionally (OAPI, ARIPO) or internationally (WIPO Lisbon system). FTAs often list protected foreign GIs and reciprocal protection for South African GIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade Marks Act route for GI protection (collective/certification mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trade Marks Act provides for the registration of a GI in the form of a collective or certification mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider trade mark registration routes (collective/certification marks) as an alternative or complementary protection mechanism for GIs under trade mark law.
